title: Camillus de Lellis (mid-July)
hook: a gambler and soldier who founded nursing brothers with red crosses on their habits

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and the brown scapular. Your line was under her mantle. What were you carrying on your shoulders? Day one thousand nine.

A young man with a bad leg and a worse habit. He's been a soldier for hire, fighting wherever there's pay. Between wars he plays cards and dice, and he loses. Tradition says he once gambled away nearly everything he owned, down to the shirt on his back. To eat, he takes work as a laborer, then as an attendant in a hospital in Rome, the kind of place for people nobody expects to get well. He's dismissed for gambling. Today, how that man ended up founding an order of nurses.
screen: `A SOLDIER FOR HIRE.` → `CARDS, DICE, AND DEBT.` → `DISMISSED FROM A HOSPITAL.`

segments.voice: Camillus de Lellis didn't turn around all at once. Tradition says the change began while he was working as a laborer for Capuchin friars, when one of them took him aside and spoke to him plainly about his life. He was taken in as a novice, but the wound on his leg, which never healed, opened again, and the friars sent him away. So he went back to the hospital, and this time he stayed. And he watched how the sick were treated. Hired attendants who didn't care. Patients left dirty, hungry, alone. He began to gather a few men who would nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child, a picture tradition gives in his own words. That little group became an order, called the Ministers of the Infirm, and Camillus became a priest. The red cross came next. His brothers wore a large red cross on the chest of their black habits, so that anyone, in a ward or a street, could see who had come to serve. They went into hospitals, into the homes of the dying, onto battlefields. Under all of it was the Gospel scene of the last judgment, where Jesus counts care for the sick as care done to himself. For Camillus, that was not a figure of speech: the patient in the bed was Christ. And the old gambler kept something from his past: he never stopped taking risks. He just changed what he bet on.
screen: `A FRIAR SPEAKS PLAINLY.` · `BACK TO THE HOSPITAL, TO STAY.` · `A RED CROSS ON A BLACK HABIT.` · `THE PATIENT IS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE CHANGED WHAT HE BET ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who nursed you. Settle, and breathe. Go back to a time you were sick or hurt. A hospital bed, a fever at home, a long recovery. Who took care of you? A nurse whose name you never learned. A parent. A friend who brought soup. Stay with their hands, their voice, what they did that you couldn't do. If you pray, you can thank God for them and ask a blessing on their work. If you don't, simply hold them in gratitude for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Camillus de Lellis. A soldier and gambler who became a priest and gathered brothers to nurse the sick, marked with a red cross on their habits.
Your line: the red cross. Today, do one plain job for someone who is sick or worn out, the kind a hired attendant skips: a fresh glass of water, a changed sheet, a dish washed. Day one thousand nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Camillus de Lellis in mid-July as a patron of the sick, nurses and hospitals, and his order, the Camillians, still serves the sick wearing the red cross.

notes: Gambling away nearly everything 'down to the shirt on his back' is given as tradition; confirm.
Turning point while working for Capuchins, refusal because of his leg wound, return to the hospital in Rome (San Giacomo degli Incurabili, not named): confirm.
'Nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child' is paraphrased as a picture his followers remember him using; confirm attribution.
Order's name given as 'Ministers of the Infirm'; red cross on black habit. No link to the later Red Cross organization is claimed; keep it that way.
Feast left as 'mid-July' per index (14 July in the general calendar; 18 July in some national calendars). Confirm.
Matthew 25 is paraphrased, not quoted, because day 1001 (Aloysius Gonzaga) already quotes 25:36.
Editor pass: reworded 'took that literally' (day 1001 used the same line about Matthew 25) in teach and trapdoor; the mother-and-only-child picture now attributed to tradition.

Audit (2026-10-01): corrected the Capuchin episode: lives say he was received as a novice and dismissed when his leg wound reopened, not refused at the door (teach, myth, fork). Carry changed from 'thank a nurse' because day 1001 (Aloysius) already had 'thank someone whose job is caring for others'; review on day 1010 updated to match.
